synopsis: Chapter 2 reports that an autonomous truck reversed into a stationary truck at Fortescue’s Christmas Creek mine in Western Australia on 11 February 2019, placing the incident within a full-autonomy mining precedent [f1372, f1826]. Press reports suggested a possible Wi-Fi coverage dropout, and a broader summary attributed the Fortescue and BHP incidents to communications and traction failures; Fortescue’s chief executive nevertheless denied that the Christmas Creek collision resulted from failure of the autonomous system [f1373, f1532, f1374]. WA DMIRS, now DEMIRS, followed up the Fortescue and BHP collisions, including interim controls [f1378, f1533, f15546]. Despite these accounts, Chapter 13 classifies the Fortescue, Rio Tinto and BHP incidents as unverified research leads to check before the real review, creating a verification gap across chapters [f11205, f11273]. Published requirement documents from Fortescue and seven other named miners were not found, leaving a separate gap in miner-specific acceptance requirements [f2599].
